title: Sushi Bus starts running in Japan, but is it a tourist trap or tourist must-do?
description: We take a trip on the world’s first conveyor belt sushi bus…and it’s like nothing we’ve ever seen before. Sushi and sightseeing tend to be at the top of the must-do list for many visitors to Japan, so what if you could combine the two and enjoy them at the same time? Well, now you […]
content:
We take a trip on the world’s first conveyor belt sushi bus…and it’s like nothing we’ve ever seen before.

Sushi and sightseeing tend to be at the top of the must-do list for many visitors to Japan, so what if you could combine the two and enjoy them at the same time? Well, now you can, thanks to the arrival of the Sushi Bus, a new two-decker restaurant bus that takes you on a tour around Tokyo while a conveyor belt filled with plates of sushi runs around the tables.

▼ In case you’re wondering, IBS Coach stands for International Business Solutions, not Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

Billed as the first bus in the world to have a sushi conveyor belt, there’s been a lot of buzz about the Sushi Bus, but does it live up to the hype? We stepped on board for a ride before tickets went on sale to find out if it was a tourist trap or a tourist must-do.

The first thing you’ll notice about the bus is its eye-catching exterior, with the entire vehicle wrapped in a giant image of two bright red tuna sushi pieces, which are said to be 12 metres (39 feet) long and 4 metres high. The bus is dubbed “Maguro-go” (“Tuna Vehicle“), with plans to introduce more buses to create a fleet from next year, and it’s a beautiful design that’ll make you feel like you’re entering a new world of sushi when you step on board.

Though the welcome sign is in English, the Sushi Bus caters to locals as well as international tourists – 70-percent of bookings in the first five days were made by Japanese people – and staff speak both English and Japanese.

▼ After making your way up a short flight of stairs, you’ll be surprised by the interior, which is like no other bus on the streets.

Running around the entire bus is a long conveyor belt, with lanterns giving the space a very Japanese vibe.

There are a variety of seating options on board the 20-seater bus, from two premium single seats at the very front…

▼ …through to a table for three…

▼…and tables for four…

▼ … and two.

▼ Every seat comes with seatbelts, which passengers are asked to wear while the bus is in operation.

As for the tables, they’re beautifully designed, at just the right height for eating, and with places in the centre console for holding the soy sauce bottle and your drinks.

Every passenger gets a free drink, with some of the choices being soft drinks, green tea, and beer.

The bus has an open-air rooftop, which gives you a fantastic view of the buildings as you glide through the streets. In inclement weather, the top closes up but it’s transparent so you can still see the Tokyo skyline.

Each tour lasts approximately 70 minutes, and takes you past some of the top spots around the city, including Tokyo Station…

▼ … Tokyo Tower…

▼ … the Imperial Palace…

▼…and the towering buildings of Ginza.

Tokyo really does look beautiful from the top of a double-decker bus, but you’ll soon find yourself looking away from the view when the sushi starts appearing on the belt.

The belt is surprisingly smooth, and there’s no fear of the sushi flying off, as the setup has been thoroughly tested to withstand even hard braking.

The all-you-can-eat extravaganza contains over a dozen sushi varieties, which may vary by day. When we visited we were able to enjoy offerings like:

▼ … egg…

▼ … crab…

▼ … salmon…

▼ … octopus…

▼ … tuna…

▼ … prawn…

▼ … squid…

▼… yellowtail…

▼ … and beef short ribs.

▼ There are also tubs filled with packs of pickled ginger and wasabi.

▼ Little plates are provided for you to empty the packs into.

▼ All the sushi is prepared in the kitchen downstairs…

▼ …and transported up to the dining area by way of a compact little elevator.

▼ Staff place the plates on the conveyor belt and keep an eye on things to make sure everything runs smoothly during the ride.

Throughout the entire tour, we couldn’t get over what we were seeing, not because of what was outside the window, but because of what was inside it.

▼ A constant stream of sushi surrounded us on the belt, like a sushi lover’s dream come to life.

While it looked wonderful, we were keen to know what the sushi actually tasted like, so we reached out and grabbed a plate of salmon from the belt.

▼ Beautifully presented on a Sushi Bus plate.

After stopping for a moment to take in the fact that we were eating sushi on a moving bus while people on the streets stared curiously at us, we dove in and found that the sushi was delicious.

Eager to try more, we grabbed the beef ribs, which were so flavourful that we found ourselves reaching for another serving immediately afterwards.

▼ Then we tried the tuna, which was another impressive offering.

Though you might think that sushi on a bus like this would be lacking in flavour, we were honestly surprised at how delicious it all was. The toppings were high quality and generously sized, and Sushi Bus says it places a lot of importance on its ingredients, sourcing them from a wholesaler at Toyosu Market who they have a business partnership with. The tuna, for instance, comes from different regions according to season, and each slice weighs 12 grams (0.4 ounces), which is about 1.5 times the amount you get at a regular conveyor belt sushi restaurant.

▼ The generous portions really do fill you up, and after five plates we were already feeling full.

▼ One of the passengers in the front seat, however, put us to shame with ten empty plates on the table.

The excitement of the tour is dialled up a notch with loud music and enthusiastic commentary from staff, who get everyone to look up at the bridges and highways that pass by within inches of the roof, giving you a unique feel for the city.

▼ The Sushi Bus is a feast for all the senses.

So…is it a tourist trap or a tourist must-do? Well, in our opinion, it’s a must-do. Sure, it’s touristy, and if you’re a local the price is pretty steep, at 16,000 yen (US$101) per person (or 22,000 yen for a premier front-row seat), but if you’re a tourist from overseas, or even outside of the prefecture, it’s an undeniably unique experience that’ll stay with you as a fun memory for years to come.

Plus, with all-you-can-eat sushi and a 70-minute trip around Tokyo that takes in some of the most iconic sights, it works out to be pretty good value, especially if you finish a lot of plates.

▼ Another bonus is the convenient pick-up and drop-off location at Marunouchi-Kajibashi Parking Lot, which is right next to Tokyo Station.

The Sushi Bus operates daily (with occasional closures for vehicle inspections and maintenance), and currently offers five tour times, with departures at 11 a.m., 1 p.m., 3 p.m., 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. Reservations can be made here, and the bus starts rolling around town from 10 October.

title: New Studio Ghibli notebooks are a beautiful reason to write and draw by hand [Photos]
description: Ghibli’s partnership with Japanese stationery brand Rollbahn expands to include three more theatrical anime. In the digital age, you don’t actually need to write by hand in order to put your thoughts into readable words, but many will say that nothing gets the creative juices flowing quite like putting pen to paper. content:
Ghibli’s partnership with Japanese stationery brand Rollbahn expands to include three more theatrical anime.

In the digital age, you don’t actually need to write by hand in order to put your thoughts into readable words, but many will say that nothing gets the creative juices flowing quite like putting pen to paper. And if artistic inspiration is the goal, being in the presence of great artwork might just make your creative process even juicier.

That philosophy is embodied by Studio Ghibli’s partnership with Rollbahn, a line of notebooks from Japanese stationery maker Delfonics. With so many memorable anime in the Ghibli filmography, the collaboration couldn’t cover all of them at once, and the line is now ready to expand with three new notebook designs, including some that don’t always get a lot of attention in the Ghibli merch world.

Starting with an unquestioned classic, though, is the new notebook saluting Castle in the Sky/Laputa. The stylized cover depicts Pazu’s daily routine of climbing onto his roof and greeting the morning (and the local flocks of birds) with a song from his trumpet.

Next we have a council of tanuki from Pom Poko, who’ve assembled to discuss how to deal with human encroachment into their living spaces, with the group expressing their approval of reviving the art of shapeshifting in order to walk among Tokyoites and observe their ways.

And finally, Tales from Earthsea, the most-maligned of Ghibli’s major theatrical releases, actually gets some love with a gorgeous cover showing Arren communing with a very important dragon in his life.

Studio Ghibli and Rollbahn are both famous for being very detail-oriented, and the notebooks have a number of thoroughly thought-out design elements. A thick, high-quality paper is used to resist ink bleeding or writing on the page’s opposite side from showing through. The pages all have a grid pattern, making them usable for writing or diagramming, and each page is perforated as well, allowing for a clean tear-out if you need to pass it off to someone else. A clear pocket at the back of the notebook also gives you a place to store any supplementary slips of paper you might need to keep nearby.

A cloth strap helps keep the book snugly closed while you’ve got it stashed in your bag when out and about, and even the colors of the binding rings and reflective text on the front are subtly differentiated to best coordinate with each cover design.

In addition to the three brand-new notebooks above, the Ghibli Rollbahn line has over a dozen different other designs for fans of My Neighbor Totoro, Spirited Away, Howl’s Moving Castle, and more, though the older notebooks fluctuate in and out of availability based on current inventory levels.

Each of the notebooks is priced at 1,430 yen (US$9.40) and can be ordered through the online store of Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku here.

title: Starbucks Japan releases new Halloween Frappuccino and drinkware, but are they worth buying this year?
description: We find out if double the cats makes for double deliciousness. While it might feel like Halloween is creeping up on us now that we’re in October, at Starbucks in Japan the festivities have already leapt up at us, with the release of a special Halloween treat called the Blackberry Yoghurt Frappuccino. Designed around the […]
content:
We find out if double the cats makes for double deliciousness.

While it might feel like Halloween is creeping up on us now that we’re in October, at Starbucks in Japan the festivities have already leapt up at us, with the release of a special Halloween treat called the Blackberry Yoghurt Frappuccino.

Designed around the theme of “Halloween Purple Cat in Mystery Forest”, where a “Phantom Purple Cat” lures you into the forest, feline motifs are key to the celebrations this year, even in the drinkware range.

▼ The purple kitty is being hidden around stores, with pawprints leading to its secret location.

With both the drink and the drinkware released at stores in Japan on 9 October, our resident Starbucks expert K. Masami decided to go all in on the feline frivolity by purchasing one of the cutest goods in the range, the Cat Glow in the Dark Double Wall Heat-Resistant Glass Cup, and asking staff to serve the Frappuccino inside it.

▼ The result turned out to be one of the cutest things she’s ever seen.

While the cup is incredibly cute, with phosphorescent sprinkles in the base and a cat with bat wings reaching for the stars, the drink itself is just as adorable. Giving it its charm is the chocolate topper, in the shape of cat ears, with two varieties to choose from – “black” or “white”.

Though she initially wanted to go for black ears, which are decidedly more spooky, Masami instead opted for white, in honour of her white cat.

Masami’s feline has her so under its spell that even her drink choices are decided by it.

▼ You…will..adore…meeee…ow”

As an ardent lover of cats and yoghurt Frappuccinos, this drink had all the elements of a dream scanrio for Masami, but what she really wanted to know was… would it taste as good as it looks?

Taking a sip, Masami’s palate was immediately enthralled by the flavours. The tartness of the berries and yoghurt made it refreshing and easy to drink, and there were even tiny blueberry pieces swimming around in the mix, adding exciting bursts of texture. The creamy milk and blackberry sauce gave every sip a delicious richness, and the balance was superbly well-crafted, making for a delicious Frappuccino.

While she was very impressed with the drink, Masami was even more impressed by the effect of the cat ears on top, which added so much cuteness that it seemed to make every mouthful even more delicious.

Both the drink and the drinkware are definitely worth buying, and the Frappuccino tasted so good that Masami vowed to return again to try it, perhaps next time with black cat ears, and without publishing it online, so her white kitty doesn’t find out about it. She’s also keen to try it with one of the recommended customisations, like chocolate chips, for added taste and texture.

▼ Always watching and reading your stories, Masami.

The Halloween Frappuccino, and the limited-edition seasonal drinkware, are available for a limited time, and only while stocks last, so be sure to get in quick to enjoy the celebrations.

description: Limited-edition exclusive comes with free goods and special prizes. Created as part of the chain’s ongoing efforts to promote pickleball in Japan, where it’s […]
content:
Limited-edition exclusive comes with free goods and special prizes.

Burger King is always looking for ways to stand out from the competition in Japan, and right now it’s doing exactly that with the release of a brand new Pickleball Burger.

Created as part of the chain’s ongoing efforts to promote pickleball in Japan, where it’s sponsored the Pickleball Japan Federation since 2025, there are two varieties in the lineup – the Pickleball Burger and the Chicken Pickleball Burger.

Each burger contains a whopping 11 pickles, as a nod to the scoring in the game, where the first player to reach 11 points wins.

Everyone’s a winner with these two burgers, as they both feature a special creamy dill sauce that balances the refreshing aromas of dill and lemon in every serving. The standard version serves up two of the chain’s signature flame-grilled beef patties, with lettuce and onions, while the chicken version swaps the beef for a chicken patty that’s crispy on the outside and juicy on the inside.

As an added bonus, the chain is giving away a free original pickleball paddle keychain for every burger purchased, although stocks are limited so you’ll want to get in quick to receive them.

Pickleball lovers and those who are new to the sport can also enjoy some extra fun with a special pickleball game on Burger King Japan’s official app. Win at the game and you’ll be rewarded with discount coupons, and if you happen to achieve a special, super-rare winning animation, you’ll automatically be entered into a lottery to win an original Burger King paddle.

The game runs from 1 p.m. on 9 October until 11:59 p.m. on 15 October. As for the burgers, they’ll be available at store locations nationwide, excluding the Kansai International Airport Terminal and racecourse branches, from 9 October. The beef Pickleball burger will be on the menu at 1,490 yen (US$9.43), or 1,790 yen as a set, while the chicken will be priced at 690 yen, or 990 yen as a set, and they’ll both be on the menu in limited quantities while supplies last.

title: Japan has convenience store fried chicken-flavor instant ramen, but does it taste like it says it does?
description: We taste-test Family Mart’s new Famichiki cup ramen, which contains no Famichiki. Like all Japanese convenience stores, branches of the Family Mart chain are stocked with dozens, if not hundreds, of delicious things to eat. That said, the star of the store at Family Mart is definitely Famichiki. This year Family Mart’s cooked-in-store fried chicken […]
content:
We taste-test Family Mart’s new Famichiki cup ramen, which contains no Famichiki.

Like all Japanese convenience stores, branches of the Family Mart chain are stocked with dozens, if not hundreds, of delicious things to eat. That said, the star of the store at Family Mart is definitely Famichiki.

This year Family Mart’s cooked-in-store fried chicken cutlets are celebrating the 20th anniversary of their debut, and they’re more popular than ever. They’re so tasty that if we’re craving fried chicken we’re probably as likely to find our feet carrying us to Family Mart as they are to KFC.

As part of the party for Famichiki’s 20th birthday, Family Mart has a couple of special treats lined up, and on October 6 they started selling a brand-new Famichiki-flavor instant ramen!

Here’s where things get mysterious, though. Famichiki Flavor Noodle isn’t cup ramen with sliced Famichiki inside of it. As a matter of fact, Famichiki Flavor Noodle doesn’t actually contain any Family Mart fried chicken, but Family Mart still promise they have the flavor of their namesake. To quote the company’s description:

“An addictively delicious cup of ramen combining spices, a fragrant, fried-flavor savoriness, and a broth brimming with umami that’ll have you feeling like you’re eating a juicy piece of Famichiki”

Family Mart is clearly confident in its new instant ramen, but can it really recreate the flavor of Famichiki? There was only one way to find out, so when we brought our 321-yen (US$2) cup of Famichiki Flavor Noodle up to the register, we asked the Family Mart clerk to also grab us a 248-yen Famichiki from the display case so that we could perform a back-to-back taste test.

Taste-testing duties fell to our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun.

▼ P.K., feeling both giddy at having a job where he gets paid to eat ramen and fried chicken, but also apprehensive at the solemn responsibility that comes with such an important assignment as this.

P.K. decided on a simple, straightforward testing protocol. First, he would take a bite of Famichiki, letting its familiarly juicy deliciousness wash over his taste buds. Then, resisting both the urge to lapse into a food coma or keep eating the Famichiki until it was all gone, he would immediately eat a mouthful of Famichiki Flavor Noodles, and see if the flavor sensation shifted.

So what did he think after tasting both?

“Yeah, they’re actually really close to each other!”

The flavors of the Famichiki and Famichiki Flavor Noodles are very similar, but what’s really remarkable is how their aromas are almost identical. Since eating cup noodles involves putting your face down into a cloud of steam rising from the broth, your olfactory sensors often play almost as big a role in how you perceive the flavor as your taste buds do. There’s a peppery meatiness to the scent of the Famichiki Flavor Noodles, and if you’ve ever eaten Family Mart’s fried chicken, it’ll feel very familiar, despite the unexpected source that it’s coming from.

However, once the broth cools down, the aroma also becomes less pronounced, since it’s no longer riding those rapidly rising hot air currents up to your nose. So as P.K. continued eating, the flavor of the Famichiki Flavor Noodle started reminding him of something else: Nissin’s Cup Noodle, specifically the flagship soy sauce-broth ramen flavor. Of course, maybe he should have seen that coming…

…since the Famichiki-flavor instant ramen is actually a joint project that Family Mart joined forces with Nissin to create.

But hey, if you’re looking for a partner to make cup ramen with, you can’t pick a better one than Nissin, and aside from tasting like Famichiki when its hot, the Famichiki Flavor Noodle tastes good all the way through to the last bite.

content:
24 years after its debut, green tea flavor gets kicked out of the Super Cup family.

With matcha being one of Japan’s favorite ice cream flavors, and confectioner Meiji’s Essel Super Cup series being one of Japan’s favorite brands of ice cream, matcha-flavored Super Cup seems like a no-brainer, right? Sadly, very soon it’s going to be a no-show in Japanese convenience stores and supermarkets, as Meiji has discontinued its green tea ice cream.

Go to the Meiji website, and you’ll see containers of vanilla, choco cookie, strawberry, cookies and cream, caramel, mint chocolate, and even blueberry rare cheesecake offered. Finding the matcha Super Cup, though, requires accessing its direct URL, and the product description now states that it’s a “discontinued product,” and that “depending on inventory levels, this product may no longer be available at [certain] retailers.” The discontinuation ends a 24-year run for the flavor, which was added to the regular Super Cup lineup in 2002.

▼ Matcha Super Cup

The exact timeline for when Meiji stopped producing matcha ice cream is a little murky. The company first stated that they’d be discontinuing the flavor back in April, but at the time gave no specific timetable for when that would be happening. The matcha Super Cup product page on the Meiji website currently says that production of the flavor ended in February of 2026, but that seems to be a typo, seeing as how that would be two months before the initial announcement of the then-in-the-future discontinuation. Some Japanese media organizations have said that Meiji ceased production of the flavor this past August, which seems like the more plausible timing.

Regardless of when Meiji stopped making matcha ice cream, though, we know that it has stopped making the flavor. Also on the “get-it-while-you-can” list is the mini-sized Super Cup combo pack containing matcha and choco cookie flavors, which Meiji also says is now limited to existing inventory, after which it’ll be gone too.

While there are a number of seasonal dessert flavors that Japan is happy to enjoy for a few weeks, then set aside until next year, matcha isn’t one of them. It’s a flavor that Japanese sweets fans joyfully consume all year long, and so the news that matcha Super Cup is now a finite resource has been met with shock and sadness by online commenters who have left lactose lamentation such as:

“I eat matcha Super Cup all the time. This is heartbreaking.”
“I’ve been eating it since I was a little kid.”
“This is a vital source of matcha for me, and now it’s gone?”
“Crushed to know I won’t be able to see you anymore, matcha Super Cup.”
“I’m honestly kind of not sure if I’m going to be OK.”
“R.I.P., matcha Super Cup.”
“Well now, with that, I’ll be dying.”

So with matcha ice cream being popular, not pigeonholed as a seasonal dessert, and no recent scandals that have turned consumers away from Meiji or ice cream in general, why is matcha being jettisoned from the Super Cup line? Meiji hasn’t made any public comment regarding the reason, but pretty much every company in Japan these days is grumbling about rising materials and ingredient costs. Matcha prices in particular are said to be rapidly increasing since it’s become the recent darling of cafes and confectioners in countries other than Japan too. Super Cup isn’t positioned as a Häagen-Dazs-like premium brand. Seen as a budget-friendly sweet snack, it generally sells for around 150 yen (US$0.95), and it may be that rising ingredient costs have made the profit margin on matcha Super Cup too thin for Meiji to think it’s worth it to continue its production.

There is still hope that Meiji will bring the matcha flavor back to the Super Cup line at some point in the future as a limited-time offering, but it’s made no announcement to that effect as of this time. It’s also possible that the company is working on a matcha flavor with which to launch a fancier, more expensive ice cream brand, although this too is just speculation.

Really, the only thing we can say for sure is that this is all further proof that when you do find yourself with the opportunity to eat matcha ice cream, you absolutely should.

title: New Sonic the Hedgehog figure costs 1 million yen, is made of Arita ware Japanese porcelain [Vid]
description: Yoyoyo says the Sega star not only has gotta go fast, he’s gotta be Arita-yaki too. Sonic the Hedgehog’s whole thing is being in motion. From his “Gotta go fast” motto to being one of the first big-name video game characters with idle animations (one of which was him impatiently tapping his foot), Sonic does […]
content:
Yoyoyo says the Sega star not only has gotta go fast, he’s gotta be Arita-yaki too.

Sonic the Hedgehog’s whole thing is being in motion. From his “Gotta go fast” motto to being one of the first big-name video game characters with idle animations (one of which was him impatiently tapping his foot), Sonic does not like to stand still.

Capturing Sonic’s personality in a stationary figure is, therefore, already a tall task, and the idea of trying to convey his characteristic kinetic energy in something as difficult to work with as traditional Japanese ceramics might seem foolish…but it’s actually awesome, as long as you have the right artists working on the project.

This amazing Sonic figurine is made using Arita-yaki/Arita ware techniques. In the 16th century, Arita, located in present-day Saga Prefecture, became the first places in Japan where porcelain art was made, and to this day Arita’s kilns produce some of the finest ceramics in Japan.

For the Sonic the Hedgehog Infinite Blue figurine, Japanese ceramics brand Yoyoyo enlisted no fewer than three Arita artist organizations. 224porcelain handled the molding, utilizing a mix of traditional and digital methods to recreate the complex contours of Sonic’s body and quills.

Things get even more intricate for the 21.3-centimeter (8.4-inch) tall figurine’s lower half, where instead of individual legs, the artists took inspiration from the blur formed by Sonic’s feet in the games when he reaches his top running speed. Not only is the infinity symbol-shaped construction incredibly detailed, the thickness of the clay had to be carefully adjusted to prevent distortion or cracking during the firing process, both of which are more likely to occur the longer or thinner a section is.

▼ The entire figurine is made up of just two parts, meaning everything you see here is one continuous piece.

After the first firing, the work-in-progress Sonic is turned over to Arita’s Riso Porcelain for glazing.

Here, again, the mix of curves and sharp angles that give Sonic his unique cute-but-edgy vibe present a serious challenge, especially since Riso Porcelain is hand-painting such traditional Japanese motifs as seigaiha (ocean waves), shippo (circles with interlocking four-pointed stars at their centers), and yagasuri (arrow feather) patterns.

The coolest thing about the coloring is the use of Arata pigment producer Fukami Shoten’s cobalt blue glaze. By delicately adjusting brush pressure and pigment concentration, Riso Porcelain lets the figure catch the light in ways that streak across Sonic’s quills, making it look like he’s sprinting with lightning speed even while the piece is standing still.

▼ Video showing the production process of the Arita ware Sonic

▼ If this is reminding you of the opening to the Ghost in the Shell anime movie, Yoyoyo also has a Japanese ceramics tie-up with that franchise.

So with all this high-class craftsmanship involved, you’ve probably already guessed that the Arita ware Sonic the Hedgehog is going to cost considerably more than the typical video game figure, and also be harder to come by. Only 50 units total will be produced and sales will be done through a lottery system, with a price of one million yen (approximately US$6,300), inclusive of tax and shipping, for buyers located in Japan. For purchasers in the U.S. Canada, England, Australia, Singapore, Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, the E.U., Norway, and Switzerland, Yoyoyo lists a price of US$7,000, with taxes and shipping fees to be calculated separately.

Five already-made figurines will also be on display at the Sonic the Exhibition-Across Generations event being held at the Ikebukuro Parco department store in Tokyo from October 9 to November 1.

Purchase applications can be made between now and October 18 (Japan time) through Yoyoyo’s website here. Delivery is estimated to take up to 10 months from the time of order, but that just gives prospective buyers more time to enjoy looking at their gold Pokémon statues.

title: If anyone needs us, we’ll be in the cardboard Japanese snack house we just built [Photos]
description: A home within a home for snacking, relaxing, and more snacking. Last year at Christmas time, our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon built a gingerbread house using a kit she purchased at housewares store Mujirushi Ryohin/Muji. She was happy with how it came out, and she might make one again once we get to the end-of-the-year […]
content:
A home within a home for snacking, relaxing, and more snacking.

Last year at Christmas time, our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon built a gingerbread house using a kit she purchased at housewares store Mujirushi Ryohin/Muji. She was happy with how it came out, and she might make one again once we get to the end-of-the-year holiday season.

But before that, Natsuno has a different edible architecture project she’s been daydreaming of: building a secret fort-style house that’s big enough for her to relax inside of, and covering it in snacks.

Natsuno got this idea from a friend who’d recently done something similar in her own home. Setting a modest budget of 3,000 yen (US$19) for herself, Natsuno knew that lumber, brick, and concrete were going to be too expensive to use as building materials, so she followed in her friend’s footsteps and decided to build her snack house out of cardboard.

After a trip to home center chain Viva Home, Natsuno had three large-sized cardboard box sheets, with exterior dimensions of 54 x 39 x 46 centimeters (21.3 x 15.4 x 18.1 inches) when folded into shape. However, instead of making them into boxes, Natsuno instead took two of the sheets and taped them together, forming the four walls for her home within a home.

Since this was going to be her special spot to relax in, she made sure that she had enough floor space for a chair, and then got to work folding her remaining cardboard sheet into a gabled roof, which she secured to the rest of the structure with more tape.

Some strategic slices with a craft knife let her cut out a door and window, and she used the trimmings to fashion a fashionable faux chimney.

OK, so now she had a house, but it wasn’t a snack house yet. Unfortunately, the cardboard and tape had cost Natsuno 1,500 yen, so she was going to need to stretch the remaining half of her budget for the snacks.

As always, when you want to get the most bang for your buck, 100 yen shop Daiso is the place to go. A shopping run at the discount chain turned up a whole bunch of wallet-friendly candidates of salty and spicy snack packs, which were just the sort of flavors Natsuno was looking for, since this was going to be a mature, for-grown-ups kind of cardboard playhouse.

Natsuno could tell that she wasn’t going to have enough snacks for total coverage of her house’s exterior, though, so she decided to focus on the roof, and positioning the house in the corner of the room meant she’d be able to leave the backside bare without hurting the aesthetics.

One by one, she taped the bags of snacks to the roof panel…

…and created this charming, mouthwatering pattern.

Natsuno was feeling pretty good with her 3,000-yen snack house, but she couldn’t help feeling the walls now looked barren if she compared them to munchies-covered roof. So she did the only sensible thing and decided to just blow past her budget and go get more snacks to cover the lower sections with too.

▼ They say your house is an investment, after all, so why not put a little more money into it?

Now in splurging mode, Natsuno didn’t limit herself to the 100-yen snack packs of Daiso, and instead allowed herself to indulge in the more luxurious fare available at supermarkets or convenience stores, adding such delicacies as beef jerky and mini dried fish cake cutlets, pistachios, and little cheeses. However, with this decadence came new construction challenges, as the larger, heavier packs of non 100-yen snacks were heavier than their Daiso counterparts, and some slid down and had to be attached using a more liberal application of tape.

Finally, after about three hours of building, Natsuno’s cardboard snack house was complete, and it was time for her to step inside!

Well, it was time for her to crawl inside, but once she was in there, it felt very cozy.

The window and roof opening keep the interior from feeling too cramped or stuffy, and also let her reach outside for more snacks when she needs them. The window even allows you to hold out your cup and ask for a refill from any family members or roommates within earshot, though there’s a non-zero-percent chance that they’ll mistake you for a Japanese horror movie ghost if you don’t give them any sort of heads-up about your building project ahead of time.

And hey, if anyone needs any convincing to pour you a drink, you can always offer them their choice of a snack from your home’s exterior in exchange for the favor.

title: Starbucks Japan serves up new Coffee Espresso Cream Frappuccino for Nighttime Dolce Coffee range

content:
A new way to have your dessert and drink it too. 

As the nights get longer and the weather starts to cool, Starbucks’ Reserve Cafes are enticing us to enjoy the evenings with three drinks inspired by the Milanese tradition of enjoying desserts and coffee at evening bars.

The drinks are a luxurious way to unwind in the evening, and two of them have been so well received by the public that they’re now permanent fixtures on the menu. The Espresso Affogato Frappuccino, which contains vanilla ice cream and espresso, has been a hit with coffee lovers, while the Opera Frappuccino is well-loved for its intense chocolate flavours and decadent dessert-like taste.

Joining the two recently introduced mainstays is a new Coffee & Espresso Cream Frappuccino, which delivers bold espresso flavours with a creamy sweetness. The Frappuccino contains a layer of espresso whipped cream at both the bottom and top of the cup, with a milky body to balance out the bitterness and create a decadent richness.

According to Starbucks, the first few sips offer more of the creamy sweetness, while the roasted aroma and deep flavour of espresso becomes more pronounced as you make your way through the drink. Those looking for even more variety can customise the drink at the Coffee Discovery Counter, with the chain recommending cacao nibs for extra texture and roasted flavour, or pink pepper for a spicy, fragrant accent.

Though they’re being billed as “Nighttime Dolce Coffees”, all three drinks can be purchased at any time at the following six Starbucks Reserve Cafe locations:

  • Shinjuku Marui Main Building 2F
  • Tokyo Skytree Town 30F
  • Daimaru Umeda B1F
  • Shinsaibashi Parco B1F
  • Nagoya Sakae Haera
  • Tenjin Business Center II

The new Frappuccino will be available in a Tall size only, priced at 900 yen (US$5.68) for dine-in and 884 yen for takeout, and will be on the menu from 9 October.

title: Experimenting with making hot sandwiches in the microwave with a device from Japan’s 3COINS
description: Can you really get crispy grill-marked sandwiches without the grill? It seems that everyone in the SoraNews24 editorial office is getting the bug for hot sandwiches, especially since they’re made easy just by using a microwave. This time around it’s our Japanese-language reporter Go Hatori who has got some wheaten cravings to satisfy, and so […]
content:
Can you really get crispy grill-marked sandwiches without the grill?

It seems that everyone in the SoraNews24 editorial office is getting the bug for hot sandwiches, especially since they’re made easy just by using a microwave. This time around it’s our Japanese-language reporter Go Hatori who has got some wheaten cravings to satisfy, and so he swung by 3COINS, Japan’s affordable lifestyle brand, and picked up the Kitinto Microwave Half Hot Sand Maker for 2,750 yen (US$17.40).

The main body resembles a glasses case, and though it is made of silicone, it feels surprisingly sturdy when picked up.

Opening it up, there were metal plates inside.

Perusing the recipes in the included booklet, all of which take about three to four minutes to cook, Go skipped past offerings like the chocolate and banana sandwich. In the end, he instead opted for a simple and classic sandwich: ham and cheese.

Go opened the body, laid down a slice of bread, and placed butter, ham, and cheese on it.

He folded it over, and closed it with the latch. The instructions say that it supports Japan’s eight-sliced loaves, but the thicker six-sliced loaves also seem to work just fine.

All that was left to do was to stand it upright and place it in the microwave for three and a half minutes at 600 watts.

The body gets ridiculously hot, so Go was extra careful when taking it out of the microwave, and when opening it.

When he did open it, what appeared before him was a magnificent hot sandwich, with the cheese still bubbling furiously in the places where it was exposed.

Go’s expectations soared, and when he took a bite…

So delicious! The surface of the bread was crispy, and the insides piping hot. Go felt that if someone were not told that it was made in a microwave they never would have expected it.

Of course, it wouldn’t be SoraNews24 without a little experimentation, so Go sandwiched a croquette bought from the supermarket into some bread and put it in the microwave at the same settings.

Once again, a truly exquisite sandwich.

The croquette was piping hot and fluffy, and the bread was crispy. To think he could get a hot croquette sandwich in a little over three minutes! Go felt like he was living in a dream.

Finally, Go tried a bite-sized pork fillet cutlet, also bought from the supermarket.

Sandwiching it with some cabbage in the bread, he put it in exactly the same way, and the result was…

▼ Perfect!

Go played with making three different types of sandwiches, and they all turned into something wonderful. He found it amazing how this hot sandwich maker could create grill marks even though it uses a microwave.

Sure, the price tag is not exactly cheap, and similar microwave hot sandwich makers are sold at other places in Japan (like Nitori), but now that he has actually used it, Go doesn’t feel like he’s wasted any money at all. In fact, he couldn’t be happier that he bought it.

All you need to do is just fill it up with your favorite ingredients and put it in the microwave. A short wait time results in a crispy hot sandwich and very little mess, as washing it was a lot easier than a frying pan or conventional hot sandwich maker. This little gadget has officially secured a spot in Go’s household, and will surely end up being used for a long time to come.

title: Tokyo train station will play Godzilla theme song as new departure melody
description: Japanese subway company adds a new soundscape to Godzilla’s Tokyo home. November 3 is a special date for fans of Godzilla as it’s known as “Godzilla Day”. First celebrated to mark the anniversary of the premiere date of the original 1954 film, Godzilla, it was eventually adopted by Toho, the film’s production company, and after it […]
content:
Japanese subway company adds a new soundscape to Godzilla’s Tokyo home.

November 3 is a special date for fans of Godzilla as it’s known as “Godzilla Day”. First celebrated to mark the anniversary of the premiere date of the original 1954 film, Godzilla, it was eventually adopted by Toho, the film’s production company, and after it was registered with the Japan Anniversary Association in 2017, Godzilla Day was officially established, representing Godzilla’s birthday.

While it’s heartening to know the kaiju has a day of its own, it also brings up a unique set of challenges, like…. what the heck do you give the King of the Monsters for his birthday? Well, subway operator Tokyo Metro has come up with a beautiful way to mark the occasion, by changing the departure melody for its trains at Hibiya Station to “Godzilla’s Theme”.

▼ Hibiya Station

Originally composed by Akira Ifukube for the 1954 film, “Godzilla’s Theme” is one of the most instantly recognisable pieces of Godzilla-associated music, with brass, strings and percussion instruments playing a relentless march that’s equal parts call-to-arms inspiring and run-for-your-life fear-inducing.

Two versions of the melody are set to be played, with different arrangements used depending on which direction you’re travelling. One arrangement will be played on platforms 1 and 3, which serves Hibiya Line trains bound for Naka-meguro and Chiyoda Line trains bound for Yoyogi-Uehara, while the other arrangement will play on platforms 2 and 4, for trains heading towards Kita-senju and Ayase.

▼ Hibiya Station is conveniently located in the heart of Tokyo.

Like all departure melodies, these ones will be played just before the train doors close and the train departs, so as long as you’re on the platform at the time you’ll be able to hear it. Tokyo Metro is asking fans to avoid lingering on the platforms though, and it’s also requesting that they avoid crowding around the speakers to record the melodies or in any other spots that might interfere with station operations.

There’s a high likelihood that fans of Godzilla will be arriving and departing by train, though, as Hibiya itself is closely tied to the kaiju, being home to Toho’s headquarters. Toho has been producing the Godzilla series for more than 70 years, and nods to the famous local company are present in two statues, one of which stands at Hibiya Godzilla Square and the other at Toho Cinemas Hibiya.

▼ Hibiya Godzilla Square

▼ The Hibiya statues are a lot smaller than this giant Godzilla atop Shinjuku Toho Building, which houses Toho Cinemas Shinjuku.

For a lot of fans, Hibiya has already established itself as Godzilla’s stomping ground, so the new departure melodies are an exciting way to dial up the kaiju vibes in the neighbourhood even further. Set to commence on 3 November, which coincides with the Japan premiere of the new movie Godzilla-0.0, the melodies are the gift that keeps on giving, as there appears to be no end date for them.

So next time you catch a train at Hibiya, be prepared for the new formidable soundscape that surrounds passengers, and don’t be surprised if you find your eyes drawn to the shadows, searching for a glimpse of Godzilla in the tunnels.

title: Video released of Pikachu’s real-world trip to space! [Video]
description: Face of the Pokémon franchise hitches a ride to the International Space Station as part of European Space Agency mission. Because Pikachu is such an iconic part of the franchise, the Pokémon games and anime have to be careful about introducing new powers for him. Sure, he always needs to be a viable candidate for […]
content:
Face of the Pokémon franchise hitches a ride to the International Space Station as part of European Space Agency mission.

Because Pikachu is such an iconic part of the franchise, the Pokémon games and anime have to be careful about introducing new powers for him. Sure, he always needs to be a viable candidate for whatever adventures are going to take place, but if Pikachu is made too powerful, he loses that quality of being an approachable, believable companion for the protagonist’s journey of growth.

So, ordinarily, Pikachu becoming a Flying-type Pokémon would be going a step too far. The following video showing Pikachu floating in mid-air is no ordinary situation, though, since it was recorded on his real-world trip to the International Space Station!

As revealed last month, a Pikachu plushie accompanied French astronaut Sophie Adenot on her trip to the ISS as part of the European Space Agency’s Epsilon mission. Pikachu even had his own custom-made ESA uniform, complete with a covering for his tail.

In the video, Adenot provides audio commentary for Pikachu’s tour of the ISS’ Nodes 1 and 2. He gets to take a look at the recycled drinking water dispenser, as Adenot explains that 98 percent of the water used on the ISS is recycled, as is its occupants’ urine, though she refrains from revealing whether or not Pikachu was asked to provide his as well. After stopping by the heavy-duty freezers used for experiment sample preservation in the node’s laboratory, Pikachu floats over into the crew quarters section of Node 2, specifically towards the area where astronauts are secured while sleeping, with Adenot hypothesizing that he’s ready for a nap.

▼ Sweet space dreams, Pikachu.

With his trip to the ISS, Pikachu joins the proud tradition of zero-gravity indicators, objects used for visual confirmation that a spacecraft has entered a zero-G environment, and also to demonstrate this status in photos and videos for people back on Earth. Despite their science-y name, zero-gravity indicators are often plushies, but Pikachu appears to the first Pokémon to fill this role.

As the video closes, Adenot mentions that Pikachu will be returning to earth before she does, but he’s still acting as a spokescharacter for the European Space Agency. To coincide with the currently ongoing World Space Week festivities, the Pokémon Center Online is offering a range of Pokémon/ESA crossover merch here, including two different astronaut Pikachu plushies.

title: Shibuya goes hard on Halloween, announces countermeasures to prevent chaos on the streets
description: Tokyo Ward clamps down as this year’s Saturday Halloween poses more dangers than the past six years.  If you’ve ever visited Shibuya’s famous scramble crossing at Halloween, you’ll know how chaotic it can be. Costumes, crowds, street drinking, and people cramming into the crossing and surrounding thoroughfares for photos and impromptu meetups are all the […]
content:
Tokyo Ward clamps down as this year’s Saturday Halloween poses more dangers than the past six years. 

If you’ve ever visited Shibuya’s famous scramble crossing at Halloween, you’ll know how chaotic it can be. Costumes, crowds, street drinking, and people cramming into the crossing and surrounding thoroughfares for photos and impromptu meetups are all the ingredients for mayhem, and after a truck was overturned by revellers in 2018, Shibuya has been doing everything it can to clamp down on the unwanted chaos.

With Halloween falling on a Saturday this year, Shibuya is preparing for more revellers than usual, and is working hard to keep things under control with a new awareness campaign that comes with the slogan “GOODBYE BAD HALLOWEEN”.

The straight-to-the-point, all-caps slogan aims to curb what Shibuya calls “Meiwaku Halloween” (“Nuisance Halloween”) behaviour, which includes drinking and smoking on the street, littering, making excessive noise and obstructing pedestrian traffic while taking photos in costume. Shibuya says this year’s celebrations pose a significatly greater risk as Halloween hasn’t ocurred on a Saturday since 2020, and it estimates that around 18,000 people will be on the streets of Shibuya Center Gai during peak times, compared to 4,200 last year, which was the lowest since records began in 2019, when there were approximately 40,000 visitors.

Though last year’s crowds were thwarted by rain, the decrease in revellers in recent years is all down to Shibuya’s concerted efforts to discourage people from making the scramble crossing area their playground during Halloween. Countermeasures now include a year-round ban on drinking alcohol on the street in Shibuya between 6 p.m. and 5 a.m., introduced in October 2024, and 62 retailers in the vicinity, including convenience stores and department stores, have been asked to refrain from selling alcohol during those hours on Halloween night.

This year also marks the first Halloween since Shibuya began collecting a 2,000-yen (US$13) fine for littering in June, with patrols being increased from the usual three teams of three to five teams of seven on Halloween.

Combined with a large police presence, plus 185 private security guards and 70 ward employees on patrol to curb bad behaviour, Halloween in Shibuya now feels less like a street party and more like a heavily regulated, slightly hostile no-go zone. While this approach has so far been successful in keeping the peace, it does come at a cost, with Shibuya saying it has spent around 74 million yen (about US$468,000) on countermeasures for this year’s Halloween. Of that, around 58 million yen is going towards station-area safety measures, 2 million yen towards rubbish collection and disposal, and 14 million yen towards public-awareness materials like flags and banners.

▼ And, presumably, this awareness video.

Despite all the countermeasures, which include temporary fencing around the famous Hachiko statue to block it from view from 6 a.m. on 30 October until 5 p.m. on 1 November, and the suspension of LUUP and Lime services around Shibuya Station from 5 p.m. on 30 October until 5 a.m. on 31 October, Shibuya Mayor Ken Hasebe isn’t entirely against Halloween.

In speaking to the press, he has been encouraging visitors to enjoy Halloween in Shibuya, just not on the streets, but by attending events organised by shopping streets, commercial facilities and clubs in the ward instead.

So the message from Shibuya this year is clear – the streets are not an all-night party venue. With police and officials out in force during the Halloween weekend, the party vibe of years past is now long gone, so you’d be better off celebrating in other parts of Tokyo instead.

description: Limited-edition drink serves up a new taste of autumn. content:
Limited-edition drink serves up a new taste of autumn.

Starbucks’ chilled cup range was first released in Japan ahead of the globe over 20 years ago, and since then it’s undergone many transformations, with limited-edition exclusives capturing the taste of the season.

Now, as we stride through autumn, the chain is giving us a new limited-edition release called the Joyful Harmony Tea Latte, which delivers chill autumn vibes with some interesting accents in flavour.

At the heart of the drink is black tea, with oolong and jasmine tea adding extra layers of complexity, combined with a good serving of milk for a creamy finish. The surprise flavour, however, is apricot, which is said to balance well with the fuller body of tea and creamy milk. Though fruity accents tend to act as a mellow counterpart in a lot of teas, Starbucks says this drink has a distinctive rich apricot aroma and a fruity taste reminiscent of perfectly ripe apricots, so you can truly enjoy the taste of the fruit.

The autumn theme is beautifully captured in the design on the cup, which features jasmine flowers, tea leaves and apricots, in gold and warm-toned hues to represent the layers of flavour and fragrance in the beverage.

While the drink can be enjoyed on its own, it’s said to pair particularly well with desserts like Sweet Potato Mont Blanc. According to the chain, the gentle sweetness and smooth texture of this dessert complements the creamy milk and fragrant tea flavours in the latte.

▼ The jasmine aroma and fruity apricot notes enhance the flavour of sweet potato, creating a very autumnal combination.

title: Tokyo government announces removal of all public phones from city’s Toei subway stations
description: Decision wasn’t made by the transportation bureau, though. Generally speaking, when the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation has an announcement to make, it has something to do with trains, buses, or some other form of public transit. One of the organization’s latest statements, though, is about phones. Specifically, it’s about public phones inside subway stations, […]
content:
Decision wasn’t made by the transportation bureau, though.

Generally speaking, when the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation has an announcement to make, it has something to do with trains, buses, or some other form of public transit. One of the organization’s latest statements, though, is about phones. Specifically, it’s about public phones inside subway stations, and how they’re going to be disappearing.

Tokyo is actually big enough that it has two different subway networks. The bureau’s announcement affects the government-managed Toei Subway system, which consists of the Asakusa, Mito, Oedo, and Shinjuku Lines, and the timetable is for none of their stations to have payphone by November of 2028 at the latest.

This isn’t a change that’s being initiated by the Tokyo government, however. Instead, it’s telecommunications operator NTT East that’s saying it wants to remove all of its phones from Toei Subway stations, and the bureau is simply passing on the company’s decision to the general public.

There’s a strong argument to be made that, in this day and age, public phones rarely serve any significant purpose. It’s not unusual for even junior high school kids to have their own smartphones, so pretty much anyone who’s going to be out and about in the city already has a way to make telephone calls, in addition to using messaging and voice chat apps for necessary communication with family, friends, classmates, or colleagues.

▼ Plus you can’t read SoraNews24 on a public phone, and just look at how annoyed this guy is by that shortcoming.

However, pay phones also have a role as disaster-relief infrastructure. Not only can they be used to contact medical and fire services, public phone networks can also be used, for free, in the case of events such as earthquakes and tsunami to make calls and contact voice message services. They provide a critical lifeline for people in disaster-stricken areas whose phones may have been lost or damaged, or who may not have access to a power supply or charging equipment after their phone’s battery runs out.

Because of that, under Japan’s Telecommunications Business Act, licensed payphone providers are required to maintain a certain concentration in areas in which they operate. Specifically, at least one public phone must be installed and in working order for every 500 square meters (5,382 square feet) in urban communities, or one phone for every square kilometer in other areas. These phone, classified as Type-1 Public Phones, should be placed either on public roads or in facilities facing public roads that the general public can access 24 hours a day.

Public phones inside rail stations, however, are not classified as Type-1 Public Phones, most likely because the stations close for several hours at night. Because of that, station phones fall into the category of Type-2 Public Phones, which can be installed or removed at NTT East’s discretion, without any need to obtain permission from the Tokyo government. As such, this appears to be a pure business decision, with NTT East no longer feeling that its in-station phones justify the cost of maintaining them compared to the undoubtedly reduced revenue they bring in.

The phones’ removal is likely to occur gradually over the next two years, and the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation says that each station will announce its removal date at least two weeks ahead of time. The bureau also recommends that those in need of a payphone utilize the search function on NTT East’s website here, though that, of course, isn’t going to be much help to anyone without a smartphone or other connectable communications device already on them.

title: My Neighbor Totoro calendar for next year can be yours right now at Donguri Kyowakoku
description: Its months don’t start until 2027, but the artwork is adorable and beautiful already. My Neighbor Totoro is unquestionably a classic of animated cinema, and that status is even more impressive when you consider that for almost the entirety of its 86-minute runtime, hardly anything is happening that pushes any sort of narrative forward. content:
Its months don’t start until 2027, but the artwork is adorable and beautiful already.

My Neighbor Totoro is unquestionably a classic of animated cinema, and that status is even more impressive when you consider that for almost the entirety of its 86-minute runtime, hardly anything is happening that pushes any sort of narrative forward. Of course, as fans know, that’s part of the film’s charm. The loose connection from one scene to another helps create a dreamlike plausibility for the anime film’s supernatural elements, and the leisurely pace of what story there is cultivates a permeating sense of nostalgia for the unhurried days of childhood.

Unfortunately, as we grow up and take on adult responsibilities, we have to adhere to more structured schedules than “Go look for forest spirits in the woods, or maybe at the bus stop later if I take a nap first.” But if you want a calendar for keeping track of appointments which will also remind you of the importance of stopping to smell the roses (or other pleasing agrarian aromas), the 2027 Totoro calendar is now available at Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku.

Each page features a scene from the anime, with ample space for writing in your schedule with pen or pencil (Studio Ghibli does love doing things by hand, after all).

There’s even a little bit of linguistics fun to be had, as the artwork for May is taken from the scene where Totoro first meets Mei, whose name is pronounced like “May” (though big sister Satsuki’s name itself means May under the old Japanese naming system for the months of the year).

Official Studio Ghibli merch designers are never ones to skimp on quality, and the calendar’s creators say they made sure to use a paper stock that’s both sturdy and easy to write on, and with a size of 51.5 x 36.4 centimeters (20.3 x 14.3 inches), the illustrations should be large enough to have some visual impact on your home or office.

We’ve still got a few months left to go in 2026, but Donguri Kyowakoku seems to be operating under the sound logic that people who buy calendars are the sort of people who like to plan ahead, and so the calendar is on sale now, priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50), and can be ordered through the chain’s online store here. Alternatively it remains available through the Ghibli museum shop here.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Halloween goods with secret glow-in-the-dark details
description: Tumblers, bottles, Bearistas and cats get us in the mood for spooky season. With Halloween now on the horizon, it’s time to stock up on spooky goods to celebrate the season, and over at Starbucks there’s a bevvy of goods to bring a dash of scary cuteness to your beverages. Designed around the concept of […]
content:
Tumblers, bottles, Bearistas and cats get us in the mood for spooky season.

With Halloween now on the horizon, it’s time to stock up on spooky goods to celebrate the season, and over at Starbucks there’s a bevvy of goods to bring a dash of scary cuteness to your beverages.

Designed around the concept of “Moon Light Halloween“, the new collection covers a wide array of drink bottles and tumblers, with sparkles, shimmers, and glow-in-the-dark details conjuring up the mysterious beauty of a moonlit evening. With over a dozen items to choose from, there’s something to suit all types of Starbucks lovers, particularly those with a soft spot for cats, as felines feature prominently in the range.

▼ Stainless Steel To-Go Bottle – Cat Light Pink, 473 millilitres (5,500 yen [US$34.78])

This bottle serves up cute cat details on the front, where a white feline sits beneath a starry sky, and on the back, where you’ll find cat-shaped customisation boxes, with a single moon thrown in.

▼ The push-button unlock feature means you won’t have to worry about spills.

▼ Stainless Steel Bottle – Glitter Light Purple, 444 millilitres (4,900 yen)

This beautiful bottle has a glittery surface that sparkles in the light, and a subdued celestial cat design for refined elegance.

▼ Stainless Steel Logo Bottle – Cat Glow in the Dark, 473 millilitres (4,950 yen)

Venture into the darkness of the night with this jet-black bottle, which cleverly incorporates black cats into the design, alongside one solitary white feline.

▼ Switch off the lights and the white cat glows in the dark, thanks to its phosphorescent coating.

▼ Stainless Steel Cold Cup Tumbler – Glitter Pink, 591 millilitres (5,450 yen)

This showstopper of a tumbler shimmers with a hot pink glittery surface, offset by cat-and-moon customisation boxes on the rear…

▼ …and a very cute straw cap that depicts a black cat sitting on the moon.

▼ Snow Globe Tumbler – Cat Glow in the Dark 355 millilitres (3,400 yen)

This tumbler looks set to be a sell-out hit, with the snow globe feature in the base containing a black cat, paw raised as if playing with the stars that swirl around it.

▼ To make things even cuter, the stars around the body of the bottle glow in the dark.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler – Cat 473 millilitres (2,800 yen)

Sip from between a cat’s ears with this sweet tumbler, which changes colour from light to dark pink with the addition of cold water.

▼ Double Wall Heat-Resistant Glass Cup – Cat Glow in the Dark 355 millilitres (3,700 yen)

▼ This glass cup also lets you drink from a cat, thanks to the adorable cat-ear lid.

The clever design gives the black cat a set of devilish bat-like wings, and when the lights are out, the scene comes to life with glow-in-the-dark confetti scattering and sparkling with every movement of the glass.

▼ Coaster – Cat (2,200 yen)

This cute coaster is as practical as it is beautiful, with its hot pink hue catching the eye, and moon-and-star details setting the scene for our black cat and cat bat.

▼ The perfect coaster for the Glass Cup.

▼ Colour-Changing Reusable Cup 473 millilitres (700 yen)

▼ This affordable cup changes colour when you pour a hot drink into it, transforming the black cat into…

▼ … a white cat!

▼ Colour-Changing Reusable Cup 473 millilitres + Reusable Cup Exclusive Drink Hole Cap Bearista Cat (1,350 yen)

Add on a cute Bearista cap and your drink will be less prone to spilling and more prone to compliments.

▼ Bearista Mini (2,750 yen)

The chain’s beloved Bearista character slips into a black cat costume for Halloween, and will look very cute when clipped onto a bag or keychain.

▼ Starbucks Mini Cup Gift with drink ticket (1,150 yen)

Those wanting to share the love have several options to choose from, with the Mini Cup Gift being arguably the cutest.

You can mimic the colour-changing effect of the larger Cold Cup Tumbler by slipping the hot pink insert in and out of the cup.

The tiny size lets you store small items like paper clips, so you can enjoy the beauty of the cup while it serves a practical purpose as part of your stationery collection.

▼ Bearista Message Gift with drink ticket (1,650 yen)

▼ For a message with soft and cuddly feels, this gift set ticks all the boxes.

It contains a drink ticket, up to the value of 700 yen for dine-in orders or 687 yen to-go, with a section where you can write a message to the recipient.

There’s also a bag for gifting, which neatly holds the card and the Bearista in batwing costume.

▼ Beverage Card with drink ticket (750 yen)

Finally, we have a shiny drink ticket, which opens up like a card for you to write a message on.

Well, that was a lovely walk in the moonlight, and now we’re definitely in the mood for Halloween. As always, the products are available for a limited time, from 9 October, and they’ll be available at Starbucks stores around Japan and online, while stocks last.

content:
The Phantom Purple Cat brings mysterious charm to two exclusive limited-edition drinks.

Now that we’re in October, Halloween is right around the corner, and Starbucks is here to celebrate with a playful new limited-edition Frappuccino inspired by a phantom cat.

The feline, known as the “Phantom Purple Cat”, sits at the centre of this year’s Starbucks celebrations, with the theme being “Halloween Purple Cat in Mystery Forest” (yes, that’s the exact official English rendering).

The elusive cat is ready to lure customers into the forest with the new limited-edition Blackberry Yogurt Frappuccino, which comes in two varieties.

▼ Black Ears Version and White Ears Version.

Common to both drinks is a fruity blueberry yogurt base, which has a sharp yet pleasant acidity and a soft, fruit-like texture. Blackberry chocolate sauce adds a deep accent in colour and flavour, and both drinks are finished with a chocolate topper shaped like cat ears, to make it seem as if the phantom cat is peeking out of the cup.

▼ The Black Ears Version uses bitter chocolate for a cooler, more grown-up look and flavour…

▼ … while the White Ears Version has a sweeter, milkier taste and a cuter look.

You can choose your cat to match your mood, but whichever feline you choose, the purple kitty will be close by watching from the sidelines, with Starbucks saying it will be hiding quietly around stores.

▼ Customers can find the purple cat by following its in-store footprints.

Joining the felines for a limited time is a special limited-edition sweet, with its dark hues and green filling matching the mood of the mystery forest.

▼ Matcha Anko Butter Chocolate Scone Sandwich

According to Starbucks, this scone resembles “a ghost sticking out its tongue“, and it contains a well-balanced sweetness, saltiness, and bitterness that pairs well with the drinks.

As an added bonus, Starbucks Rewards members who purchase one of the cat-eared Frappuccinos will be able to receive a free chocolate chips customisation by using the app or presenting the designated QR code at the register from 9-15 October.

Both drinks will be available in a Tall size only, priced at 730 yen (US$4.60) for dine-in or 717 yen for takeout. They’ll be on the menu for a limited time from 9 October.

title: Wendy’s Japan goes big with new limited-edition Mega Wendy’s, but is it worth the calories?
description: Sometimes Japanese portion sizes are small… and sometimes they look like this. Wendy’s is often overlooked in Japan, but right now it’s towering over the competition with a new burger called MEGA Wendy’s. The all-caps in the name is certainly warranted, because it’s even bigger than the three-patty Wendy’s Burger USA Triple (known as “Dave’s […]
content:
Sometimes Japanese portion sizes are small… and sometimes they look like this.

Wendy’s is often overlooked in Japan, but right now it’s towering over the competition with a new burger called MEGA Wendy’s. The all-caps in the name is certainly warranted, because it’s even bigger than the three-patty Wendy’s Burger USA Triple (known as “Dave’s Single” in the U.S.), with four extra beef patties and four slices of cheese giving it a total of seven patties and an astonishing 2,614 kilocalories.

Our reporter Kouhey has taken on all kinds of big burger challenges over the years, but this one looked so formidable that he spent a long time wondering whether he should even take it on. However, after finding out that the new burger was released nationwide to commemorate its appearance on TV, he realised he may never get the chance to take on such a heavyweight again, so he shrugged off his concerns and headed out to his nearest branch.

After arriving at the Iidabashi Ramla store, located in the Iidabashi Ramla commercial complex next to JR Iidabashi Station, he walked over to one of the self-service kiosks and blinked in surprised when he saw the burger on the menu, branded with a “New Product” tag and standing there like a meat tower.

▼ His eyes widened further when he saw the price – the burger, on its own, was a whopping 3,670 yen (US$23.36).

This was the first time he’d seen a burger this expensive at a chain restaurant, and it was so pricey that he had to check whether he had enough in his wallet to cover it. Fortunately, he did, so he ordered it as part of a drink set, bringing the total to 3,910 yen.

Looking at the stats, the MEGA Wendy’s is approximately 14 centimetres (5.5 inches) tall and weighs 900 grams (1.98 pounds). This was way bigger than Burger King’s four-patty Crown The One Pounder, which Kouhey previously battled with in 2023, so he felt slightly wary of this new opponent, which was in a totally different weight class.

After about five minutes of waiting, Kouhey’s number was called, and when he took the tray over to his table, he felt his muscles activate under the weight of the tray.

▼ “What the heck is this?!” He thought to himself. “Is it an iron ball?”

Even while wrapped in its paper, the burger was already a massive round mass. Looking closely, he could see the words “CHICKEN” and “SPECIAL” printed on the paper, and it was so large that it had been wrapped around the burger several times.

▼ Picking it up, it was seriously heavy – like something you could use for strength training.

Carefully unpeeling the wrap… the monster revealed itself.

▼ Meat, meat, meat, meat, meat, meat, meat!!!

It truly was a wall of meat. Seven patties were stacked up on top of each other, pushing the top bun upwards. When he lifted the bun, he could see onions, ketchup and lettuce sitting above it all, giving it the character of a burger, but with a mountain of meat underneath.

Looking closely, Kouhey discovered a good amount of cheddar cheese between the patties, and when he gently pried them apart, the melted cheese looked nice and gooey.

Though all the components of a good burger were clearly present, Kouhey was surprised at how the buns seemed so miniscule – the top and bottom buns were completely outdone by the seven patties between them.

▼ Then there was the burger packaging, which was enormous when he spread it out, giving you an idea of just how big the burger was.

At 14 centimetres tall, this is a seriously tall burger, and it was a tall order to eat. As the battle between man and burger began, Kouhey, gripped the burger firmly and brought it up to his mouth…

▼ …but the thing was so huge that he could only eat the meat.

No matter how much he ate, every mouthful consisted of nothing but meat, and sometimes a little cheese. Every now and then, a hint of bun or a skerrick of onion would timidly make its way into the mix, but it felt less like eating a hamburger and more like eating a lump of meat with cheese sandwiched in between.

About halfway through, he took a breather and paused to check the cross-section.

▼ There was still a lot left.

As a seasoned big burger professional, Kouhey knew he was now entering the “flavour-change zone”. This is what he likes to call the stage where your palate gets so tired of the monotonous flavours that you need to add a little something extra to keep you going until the end, and to help with his, he added some habanero sauce, which he’d picked up from beside the register.

Drizzling it over the cross-section of the patties, he wondered what kind of difference the sauce would make to the flavour profile.

▼ Whoah. This was actually good.

The spiciness and acidity enlivened his palate, lifting it from all the meat and cheese that had been weighing it down. After the endless procession of meat, the sauce provided some welcome relief, helping him through the second half. Although the meat remained the star of the show, there was no stopping Kouhey’s momentum now, so it didn’t take long for the tower, which had once seemed impossibly tall, to shrink down to a size that fit in the palm of his hand.

▼ A few more bites and finally, the end came into view.

▼ Then, the final bite.

▼ K.O.!

With his belly now full, Kouhey let a smile drift across his face as he reveled in his sense of achievement at having devoured the beast. Looking back at the timestamps on his photos, he found that it’d taken about 18 minutes between him receiving the tray and folding away the burger wrap at the very end of the meal. Although he had to stop repeatedly to take photos, he’d completed the task in good time, and he could confidently say this is the most amount of meat he’s ever eaten in a single sitting.

In the end, the MEGA Wendy’s was less a hamburger and more of a meat-eating challenge. If you feel ready to take on the challenge, be sure to stop by Wendy’s soon as it’s only a limited-time menu item, and come prepared with an empty stomach to take on the beast.
